newsitem.title: THAILAND: Rice - Thai trade divided on flood damage.
newsitem.headline: Rice - Thai trade divided on flood damage.

text.p: Thai rice traders were divided on the damage inflicted on farms by rising floodwaters as regional rice prices held at firm levels on the back of robust demand, traders said on Thursday.
"Flood is better than drought. (The) rice paddy in lowlands is definitely affected by floods, but at the same time the output in highlands is likely to rise," one Thai trader said.
"The rice output is likely to drop, but not sharply. I hope the floods will not put further pressure on rice prices. They are already a bit too expensive," another Thai trader added.

Monsoon floods in Thailand became a factor in pushing up rice prices in the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) on Monday because of concern over the fate of its crop. Thailand is the world's leading rice exporter.

The thin market was pressured by news of the floods, trade sources said. Thai benchmark 100 percent grade B rice was quoted around US$330-340 a tonne FOB Bangkok, compared with $320-340 per tonne last week.
The Interior Ministry has said that 556,919 hectares of farmland were damaged by floods, 397,859 hectares of which were rice fields.
Exporters engaged in hand-to-mouth buying to cover their immediate commercial requirements as only several ships were at Bangkok port loading rice for transport to China, Syria, Africa and Hong Kong.
Growing demand from Russia and the Middle East, on the other hand, pushed up prices of rice exports from India, which expects a good winter crop, traders and analysts said.
"Firm demand from Russia and Middle East countries had pushed up Indian higher grades (five percent broken) rice export prices by nearly $10," said Prem Garg, a leading New Delhi foodgrains exporter.
Garg said the export price of this kind of rice had risen to $300 a tonne from $290 a week ago. Traders said the price of Indian rice was on par with rice of a similar variety in Vietnam.

"But Russia has more than $10 dollars freight advantage if it buys from India (rather) than Vietnam," Garg said, adding Middle East countries can also take advantage of lower freight rates on purchases from India.
Garg did not say what quantities had been contracted with Russia or the Middle East countries.
Analysts said India's winter output was expected to be nearly 72 million tonnes, marginally up from last year's level of 71 million. The winter harvest began in early October.
Government officials had earlier estimated India's winter rice production at a record 75 million tonnes.
"Less output is expected than earlier anticipated due to the marginal damage to the rice crop in Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka," said one analyst.
The southern state of Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka contribute nearly 15 percent of the country's total rice output.
Traders said Indian five percent broken non-Basmati rice was currently quoted at $300 per tonne FOB, 10 percent broken at $280, 15 percent at $255 and 25 percent at $240.
"According to trade sources, traders have signed deals to export nearly half a million tonnes of rice in November," an official in a leading Delhi foodgrains export firm told Reuters.
India exported nearly 5.5 million tonnes of rice in 1995/96 (April-March), against a target of three million tonnes. India is now the biggest exporter of rice after Thailand.

In Vietnam, rice prices have remained stable this week in steady but active trading, dealers said. Five percent broken grade was being quoted at around the $265 per tonne mark FOB Saigon Port, unchanged from a week earlier.
"It remains a major origin as current Vietnam prices are low," said one regional dealer.
Vietnam's Lao Dong (Labour) newspaper reported on Wednesday that some 12,500 tonnes of low grade 25 percent broken would be shipped to Sri Lanka in the last week of October.
